name: PSM SEO Site Console
author: brodricklacyhudson

sections.description:
Your website is a planet. The Pods map it.

PSM SEO Site Console docks a complete, private first SEO toolkit inside your WordPress dashboard. Everything runs in your browser and on your own server. Nothing you type is uploaded to us, ever.

The rooms

  • Structure. Send the Pods to your site and they chart every path in a top down sitemap or a rotating 3D galaxy, surface orphan and broken pages, and hand back a letter grade. The same site always earns the same grade, so you can measure a fix.
  • Presence. One canonical business profile, checked field by field against the 11 directories that matter: Google Business Profile, LinkedIn, Bing Places, Apple Business Connect, Clutch, and more. Your data stays on your device.
  • Redirector. Broken pages found by the crawl become ready 301 rules, exportable as .htaccess directives or JSON.
  • Schema. Generate valid JSON-LD from your business profile, and inspect the structured data any page already ships.
  • Repairs. Every fault the crawl found, worst first, each with its cause and its fix, plus a brief to paste into an AI assistant.
  • Campaigns. Tagged links, so you can tell which channel actually brought someone.
  • Reports. What changed between two real crawls, and a report you can print or save as a PDF.
  • Tracking and Search engines. Inside your dashboard only: your own tag and its health, proving the site is yours to each search engine, instant indexing, and country versions.

The mothership features

  • Automatic structured data on your site: one clean schema graph covering your business entity, articles, products, FAQ, events, and video, each type toggleable.
  • A virtual XML sitemap served at /sitemap.xml with zero physical files written to disk.
  • Insights: your own first party, anonymous usage analytics with charts: headline stats, a six month trend, per surface totals, and a feature leaderboard, all on your server. No third party analytics, no identifiers, and Do Not Track is honored.
  • Cerebro: optional server side event forwarding to your own Google Tag Manager server container, plus a downloadable GTM recipe.
  • Webhook broadcasts of crawl findings to Zapier, Make, or n8n.
  • A diagnostics tab that decodes every error code in plain language.

Free and paid

This plugin is free and fully functional: crawl and grade your site structure, the complete Presence workflow, all schema tools, the virtual sitemap, Insights, Cerebro, webhooks, and the Search Console connection. Nothing here is gated behind a purchase. Planet Social Console Pro is a separate add on, installed alongside this plugin from our own site, that adds higher crawl caps and the large site skeleton crawl for very large sites.

Security and your responsibility

Planet Social Marketing is an independent developer. This plugin is not made, reviewed or endorsed by WordPress or the WordPress Foundation.

It connects your site to other services with keys and access you provide, such as a Google sign in, API keys and connect keys. Those are powerful: anyone who holds one can act as your site with that service. Keep them private, replace any key that leaks, and remove connections you no longer use.

We check every release against WordPress coding and security standards with the official Plugin Check tool from WordPress, and fix what it finds before we ship. No software is flawless, though, and this plugin is provided as is, without warranty, under the GPL.

We are not responsible for the security of your own browser, devices, hosting, accounts or passwords, or for faults in other plugins and services. Keep WordPress, your plugins and your browser up to date, use strong passwords and two factor sign in, and connect only services you trust.

Privacy

Crawls run in your browser. Your business profile lives in your browser’s local storage. The plugin stores its settings in a single option row and removes everything on uninstall. Optional anonymous feature counts go only to your own site’s endpoint. Full policy: https://planetsocialmarketing.com/privacy

External services

This plugin talks to the outside services listed below, each only for the purpose described. Your crawl results, page content, and business profile are never sent to us. Every service other than the web font is off until you choose to use it.

  1. Google Fonts (fonts.googleapis.com, fonts.gstatic.com).

The docked console interface loads its typefaces (Fraunces, Inter, and JetBrains Mono) from the Google Fonts CDN when you open the console screen in wp-admin. This is a request for font files only; your browser sends the standard request headers (including your IP address) to Google to fetch the fonts. No plugin data, page content, or profile information is included. If you prefer no external font request, the interface falls back to your system fonts.

This service is provided by Google LLC. Terms: https://policies.google.com/terms . Privacy: https://policies.google.com/privacy

  1. Google APIs, optional and off until you enable them.

If you connect Google on the Credentials tab, your browser goes to accounts.google.com so you can approve access, and the plugin exchanges, refreshes and, when you disconnect, revokes the resulting tokens at oauth2.googleapis.com. With that connection it reads your own verified Search Console property from www.googleapis.com, and asks searchconsole.googleapis.com how Google sees a page when you inspect one. With the same connection it reads your own Google Analytics property: analyticsadmin.googleapis.com says which properties your account has and which web address each one measures, so the plugin can find the one that belongs to this site, and analyticsdata.googleapis.com returns visit counts, bounce rate, average visit length, where visits and visitors came from, and anything bought, for whole days only. Every one of these calls only reads: the plugin never creates, changes or deletes anything in Analytics or Search Console, and no page content or visitor record leaves your site. Sites connected before Analytics was added granted Search Console only and keep working; reading Analytics needs you to press Connect Google again and approve it. If you set up Cerebro server side tagging, the events you select are forwarded to the Google Tag Manager server container that you own and control, at the address you enter. If you enter your Google Tag Manager container ID and turn on Load GTM on the site, the plugin loads that container from www.googletagmanager.com on your front end, the same snippet you would otherwise paste by hand. All of these stay dormant until you configure them, and you can turn them off at any time. Data flows only between your own site and your own Google account.

This service is provided by Google LLC. Terms: https://policies.google.com/terms . Privacy: https://policies.google.com/privacy

  1. Google Tag Manager API, optional and off until you switch on Tag Manager writing.

Only if you switch on Tag Manager writing under Cerebro and connect Google does the plugin ask Google for permission to edit your Tag Manager containers (the tagmanager.edit.containers scope). With it, the plugin asks tagmanager.googleapis.com which containers your account can edit, so you can pick one by name. Then, only when you press Build the tags, it creates one new workspace in the container you chose and adds a GA4 configuration tag, plus a trigger and an event tag for each event in the set you picked. What is sent is the container address, your GA4 measurement ID and those tag and trigger definitions. It never publishes: the plugin does not ask for permission to publish a container, so nothing it creates reaches your visitors until you review the workspace in Tag Manager and publish it yourself. It never changes or deletes a tag or trigger that was already there. Show me what it would build lists the same objects and sends nothing. While the switch is off, the permission is not requested at all.

This service is provided by Google LLC. Terms: https://policies.google.com/terms . Privacy: https://policies.google.com/privacy

  1. Stape, optional and off until you connect it.

If you paste a Stape API key on the Credentials tab, the plugin asks Stape which server containers your account has and what addresses they answer on, so you can pick one by name instead of copying a long address by hand. Only the key is sent, as a header, to api.app.stape.io or api.app.eu.stape.io depending on the region you choose. Every call is read only: the plugin never creates, changes or deletes anything in your Stape account. No page content, crawl result or visitor data is involved. The key is stored encrypted with your site keys, and Disconnect removes it.

This service is provided by Stape. Terms: https://stape.io/terms-conditions . Privacy: https://stape.io/privacy-notice

  1. Google PageSpeed Insights, optional and off until you connect it.

If you paste a PageSpeed Insights API key on the Credentials tab, then each time you press the check button the plugin sends one page address and the key to www.googleapis.com and receives back how fast that page is. Google answers with two different things and the plugin keeps them apart: what real Chrome visitors experienced over the last 28 days, which only exists where enough people visited, and a simulation run on Google’s own hardware. Nothing is sent unless you press the button, and only the address of a page on your own site is ever sent.

This service is provided by Google LLC. Terms: https://policies.google.com/terms . Privacy: https://policies.google.com/privacy

  1. IndexNow, optional and off until you switch it on.

IndexNow tells search engines that a page on your site changed, so they read it again sooner instead of waiting for their next crawl. While it is switched on, the plugin sends a request to api.indexnow.org when a public post is published, unpublished or moved to the trash, when the Planet Social Redirector plugin creates a permanent redirect (the old address and the new one), and when you press one of the IndexNow buttons in the console (your home page, or your twenty most recently published posts). Each request carries your site’s host name, the addresses of those pages, your site’s IndexNow key and the address of its key file. The key is not a secret: the plugin publishes it at your site’s root so the engines can confirm the request came from your site. The same address is not sent again within an hour. IndexNow shares each submission with the search engines taking part, such as Microsoft Bing, Yandex, Seznam and Naver. No page content and no visitor data is sent.

IndexNow is run by its sponsors, Microsoft, Yandex and Seznam.cz. Terms: https://www.indexnow.org/terms . Privacy: the Privacy section of the same page, https://www.indexnow.org/terms

  1. Webhook automation, only the address you enter.

If you paste a webhook URL on the Credentials tab, for example a Zapier catch hook at hooks.zapier.com or a Make or n8n webhook, the plugin POSTs a small JSON summary of crawl findings to that address when a broadcast fires. Nothing is sent until you enter a URL, and it goes only to the endpoint you chose, under that service’s own terms. Zapier terms: https://zapier.com/legal/terms-of-service . Zapier privacy: https://zapier.com/privacy

  1. Crawl relay, only the address you enter.

Crawling the site this plugin is installed on happens directly in your browser. Browsers block reading other sites that way, so to crawl a different site, such as a client’s, you can run a small relay of your own and enter its address under Advanced in the console. The console then sends the address of each page it wants to read to your relay, which fetches that page from the site you chose and hands it back. Nothing goes to a relay until you enter one. The setup guide uses a free Cloudflare Worker, at an address like your-worker.workers.dev, which is also the hint shown in the empty field. Cloudflare terms: https://www.cloudflare.com/website-terms/ . Cloudflare privacy: https://www.cloudflare.com/privacypolicy/

  1. Business directory links, in the Presence room.

The Presence room lists eleven business directories as ordinary links. The plugin never connects to them, fetches from them or sends them anything. A directory opens in a new tab only when you click it, and from then on you are on that site under its own terms.

  • Google Business Profile, business.google.com. Terms: https://policies.google.com/terms . Privacy: https://policies.google.com/privacy
  • LinkedIn Company Page, www.linkedin.com. Terms: https://www.linkedin.com/legal/user-agreement . Privacy: https://www.linkedin.com/legal/privacy-policy
  • Bing Places, www.bingplaces.com. Terms: https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/servicesagreement . Privacy: https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/privacy/privacystatement
  • Apple Business Connect, businessconnect.apple.com. Terms: https://www.apple.com/legal/internet-services/terms/site.html . Privacy: https://www.apple.com/legal/privacy/en-ww/
  • Clutch, clutch.co. Terms: https://clutch.co/terms . Privacy: https://clutch.co/privacy
  • Yelp for Business, biz.yelp.com. Terms: https://www.yelp.com/static?p=tos . Privacy: https://www.yelp.com/static?p=privacy
  • Facebook Business Page, www.facebook.com. Terms: https://www.facebook.com/terms/ . Privacy: https://www.facebook.com/privacy/policy/
  • Foursquare, business.foursquare.com. Terms: https://foursquare.com/legal/terms . Privacy: https://foursquare.com/legal/privacy
  • YellowPages, accounts.yellowpages.com. Terms: https://www.yellowpages.com/about/legal/terms-conditions . Privacy: https://www.yellowpages.com/privacy
  • Better Business Bureau, www.bbb.org. Terms: https://www.bbb.org/terms-of-use . Privacy: https://www.bbb.org/privacy-policy
  • Nextdoor Business, business.nextdoor.com. Terms and privacy: Nextdoor’s Member Agreement and Privacy Policy, in the Legal section of the Nextdoor Help Center, which the foot of nextdoor.com links to.
  1. Other links.

These are ordinary links too. Nothing is sent until you click one.

  • The Pods app on Google Play, play.google.com, and on the Amazon Appstore, www.amazon.com. Google Play terms: https://play.google.com/about/play-terms/index.html . Google privacy: https://policies.google.com/privacy . Amazon conditions of use: https://www.amazon.com/gp/help/customer/display.html?nodeId=GLSBYFE9MGKKQXXM . Amazon privacy: https://www.amazon.com/gp/help/customer/display.html?nodeId=GX7NJQ4ZB8MHFRNJ
  • Google’s Rich Results Test at search.google.com, and your own Google Analytics and Tag Manager at analytics.google.com and tagmanager.google.com, under the Google terms and privacy policy in item 2.
  • The Schema Markup Validator at validator.schema.org, part of schema.org. Terms: https://schema.org/docs/terms.html . The validator publishes no separate privacy policy.
  • Our own site, planetsocialmarketing.com, for the field manual, the relay guide, plans and our policies. Terms: https://planetsocialmarketing.com/terms-of-service/ . Privacy: https://planetsocialmarketing.com/privacy/

Addresses on schema.org, www.w3.org and www.sitemaps.org that appear in the code are the names of vocabularies and formats written into your pages and your sitemap; the plugin never contacts them. Addresses on example.com and other reserved example names appear only as hints inside empty fields.
sections.faq:
Does my data leave my site?

No. Crawls run in your browser, the business profile stays in browser storage, and the optional usage counts post to your own site’s REST endpoint, not ours.

What are orphan pages and why do they matter?

Orphans are pages with no internal link pointing to them, the quiet failure of most site migrations. AI assistants answer questions by crawling links and sitemaps, so a page no path reaches never gets cited in an AI answer.

Can the Pods crawl sites other than mine?

Crawling the site the plugin is installed on always works. Browsers block fetching other domains, so crawling a different site requires a small relay you can run free on Cloudflare; the in app guide walks you through it in about a minute.

What happens to my settings if I uninstall?

Everything is removed. The plugin keeps its entire configuration in one option row and deletes it, along with its rewrite rules, on uninstall. No ghost data.

Is the paid tier required?

No. The free features work forever. For bigger sites, a separate add on installed from our own website, Planet Social Console Pro, raises the crawl caps and adds the large site skeleton crawl. Pricing and details live at planetsocialmarketing.com.
sections.changelog:
2.48.3

  • The plugin header now declares Requires at least: 6.0 and Requires PHP: 7.4, the same as this readme, so WordPress will not activate the plugin where it cannot run.
  • Keys and the Google connection are stored encrypted with PHP’s OpenSSL extension. On a server without it, the Credentials tab now says so and refuses to save, where before it stored nothing without a word.

2.48.2

  • Renamed to PSM SEO Site Console, with the slug and text domain psm-seo-site-console that WordPress.org assigned. Same features, same settings, same code.
  • Readme: Nextdoor’s Member Agreement and Privacy Policy are named rather than linked, because the Help Center they live in sends an incomplete certificate chain that link checkers report as broken.

2.48.0

  • Security: an uploaded verification file is no longer served the way it arrived. Each one is rebuilt when it is requested and escaped as it prints: a text file through esc_html, an HTML file through wp_kses with only the tags a verification page uses, and Bing’s BingSiteAuth.xml from its own template. The old check refused script tags but let an event attribute through. A file that fits none of those shapes is refused with the reason, and one stored by an earlier version that no longer fits is marked Not served.
  • Open Graph and Twitter tags, the region switcher template tag and the Android app links file now escape at the moment they print.
  • Fixed: the version this plugin stamps on its own files had been stuck at 2.38.2 since that release, so a browser or a host’s cache could keep showing an older console after an update, and the console reported the wrong version. It follows the real version again, and the build now refuses to package if the two disagree.
  • The IndexNow guard that stops the same address being sent twice in an hour is stored under the plugin’s own prefix, so uninstall removes it too.
  • Removed the pods_render_language_switcher and pods_get_language_switcher aliases. Call psconsole_render_language_switcher and psconsole_get_language_switcher.
  • UpCity closed in late 2025 and its address now leads nowhere, so Foursquare takes its place in the eleven Presence directories.
  • The console in this plugin no longer tries to reach a desktop service on your own computer after a crawl. That service is part of our own tooling, not something you have, and current Chrome asks your permission before a website may talk to your computer.
  • Opened outside your dashboard, the console sends its anonymous feature counts to the site it runs on. One fallback pointed at planetsocialmarketing.com.
  • Fixed: the AI crawler switches on the Settings tab showed no choice selected, so the screen never said what was saved, and WP_DEBUG reported three undefined variables. Found by testing on a clean install with WP_DEBUG on.
  • The console in this plugin no longer registers the app’s offline service worker. That file lives on our own site, not in the plugin, so every dashboard logged a 404 for it.
  • Readme: External services names every address the plugin contacts or links to, what is sent and when, and each service’s terms and privacy policy, including IndexNow.

2.47.3

  • Readme: the External services section now describes the Tag Manager API that tag building uses, what is sent and when, and that the plugin never asks for permission to publish. Its numbering is fixed.

2.47.2

  • Fixed: the Commander helper in the dashboard corner showed as a plain white box and did nothing. Since 2.44.2 its styles and script were written with a newline PHP does not turn into a newline, so the browser read every style rule after the first as belonging to an element that does not exist, and refused the script outright. The alien is drawn and the briefing opens again.
  • Fixed: the same fault had left the Pods SEO box in the post editor unstyled: the character counters lost their colours and an empty image preview showed as a broken box.
  • Fixed: the Home tab showed two Commanders, the dashboard’s own and the one inside the docked console. The console carries its own, with a briefing for every room, so the dashboard one now stands down on Home and stays on every other tab.
  • Fixed: the Arcade room showed your site’s “Page not found” page instead of the game. The console looks for the game beside itself and the plugin never shipped it, so the request fell through to WordPress. It ships now. This copy reports no analytics: inside your dashboard it has no business sending game events anywhere.
  • Fixed: on a phone, some words in the Benchmark, crawler and Calendar tables were split in two. The earlier fix for tables running off the screen let a column shrink to a single letter wide. Now a column never gets narrower than its longest word, and only a long web address may break mid way.

2.47.1

  • Fixed: on a phone the Benchmark table lost the compared site’s column off the right, the AI crawler table lost the crawler names off the left, and the directory list put its second column off screen with the Sync button cut in half.
  • All three were the same mistake in three places. Something with a minimum width that cannot shrink, a cell set never to wrap, an address with no space in it to break at, a card name set never to wrap, sat inside a container assumed able to shrink. A width of 100 percent cannot go below that minimum, so the panel grew instead and the far side left the screen.
  • Measured rather than eyeballed: at 320 pixels the crawler table was 117 pixels wider than the space it had. It now fits at every width from 320 up.

2.47.0

  • New: two switches that write AI crawler rules into your robots.txt, on the Settings tab. The console could already tell you which crawlers a site turns away. Now it can change it, without anybody editing a file.
  • They are separate on purpose, because there are two kinds of AI crawler and one blanket rule takes out both. Refusing the ones that collect pages to train a model is a licensing decision about your own work. Refusing the ones that fetch a page so an assistant can quote you, with a link back, just removes you from the answer and leaves the citation to a competitor.
  • Three states, not two. Leave alone writes nothing and keeps whatever your robots.txt already says. Allow writes an explicit rule, which overrides a blanket Disallow that something else wrote, because a crawler obeys the group that names it and only falls back to the star group when none does. Ask not to turns them away.
  • It says when it cannot work. If a robots.txt file sits at your web root, WordPress never serves the one these switches write, and the card says so rather than looking like it did something.
  • New: a dry run for the tag builder. Show me what it would build lists every tag and trigger with the name it would have in your container, and calls nothing. It is there so that testing does not need a second container.
  • The dry run and the build read the same list, so a preview cannot drift away from what actually gets made.
  • Fixed: building tags stopped with a name error before anything was created. The workspace name carried a timestamp containing a colon, and Tag Manager refuses a colon in a name. Every name now passes a guard on the way out.
  • Fixed: a refused Google sign in said only to check the OAuth app configuration, discarding the reason Google gave. It now reports what Google said and names the fix for the common ones, including the missing Tag Manager permission, which breaks the whole sign in rather than only Tag Manager.

2.46.2

  • Fixed: the field guide said the console has four rooms. It has eleven. Four is how many seats the curved bar on a phone has, which is a fact about the bar, not the console, and Repairs, Clients, Calendar, Benchmark, Campaigns and Reports were never added to the list.
  • Fixed: the answer about the field manual said eleven pages. The current edition is sixteen.

2.46.0

  • New: which AI crawlers a site lets in, read from its own robots.txt, in the Schema room and in the printed report. It works on any site you crawl, including a prospect’s, because robots.txt is public.
  • It separates the two kinds that get confused. Some crawlers collect pages to train a model, and saying no to that is a decision about your own work. Others fetch a page so an assistant can quote it, with a link back to you. Blocking the second protects nothing and removes you from the answer.
  • Most sites that block AI do it with one blanket rule and take out both. The report says so in a sentence rather than handing you a checklist.
  • It reads robots.txt the way a crawler does: a bot obeys the group that names it and only falls back to the star group when none does, so a blanket rule does not govern a bot with its own group.
  • It says “asked not to”, never “blocked”. robots.txt is a request that well behaved crawlers honour, and claiming otherwise would sell a lock that is really a sign.

2.45.0

  • New: build your GA4 tags straight into your own Tag Manager container. It creates a GA4 configuration tag, plus a trigger and an event tag for view_item, add_to_cart, begin_checkout, purchase, generate_lead and sign_up.
  • It creates a workspace and stops. Nothing reaches your visitors until you open Tag Manager, look at what was built, and publish it yourself. It cannot publish even if you asked it to: the plugin requests permission to edit a container and deliberately does not request permission to publish one.
  • It only ever adds. Everything it writes carries the Cerebro name, and it never reads, changes or deletes a tag you already had.
  • Tag Manager access is off by default and has to be switched on. Asking Google for a permission your own Cloud project does not list makes the entire connection fail, including Search Console and Analytics, so this one is opt in on purpose.
  • What a Cerebro tag is now lives in one place, shared by the exported container recipe and the new builder, so the two cannot drift apart.
  • Six sets to choose from instead of one list for everybody: a bit of everything, online shop, services and enquiries, content and publishing, video and audio, and downloads. A law firm has no cart and a magazine has no checkout, and the old list assumed both.
  • Every event name is one of Google’s own recommended events, so GA4 reports on them without you building a custom report.
  • Where a set contains something GA4 already measures by itself, like file downloads or video progress, the screen says so before you build. Enhanced Measurement is on by default, and a tag for one of those counts it twice.
  • Building a tag does not create the event. Your site still has to push it, and which events matter is a decision about your business that no plugin can make for you. The screen says that too.

2.44.3

  • Three classes that were named Pod_IndexNow, Pod_Locale and Pod_Verify are now PSConsole_IndexNow, PSConsole_Locale and PSConsole_Verify, matching the eighteen other classes in the plugin. PHP stops with a fatal error if two plugins declare the same class name, and those three were short enough to collide with somebody else’s. Nothing outside the plugin referred to them, so nothing else changes.

2.44.2

  • Fixed: the plugin printed a style tag and a script tag straight into the admin in three places instead of going through the enqueue API. The commander helper and the Pods SEO meta box now register a handle and attach their CSS and JavaScript with wp_add_inline_style and wp_add_inline_script, the way the rest of the plugin always has. What is printed is unchanged; how it gets there is not.
  • Fixed: the readme pointed at a Stape terms page that no longer exists. It points at the one that does.

2.44.1

  • Fixed: the calendar could schedule “Expand this page, about -1 words”. Minus one is what this console stores for a page whose word count was never measured, and the thin pages check accepted it as thin. It now requires a real count above zero, which is what the Opportunities check has always done.

2.44.0

  • New: a Benchmark room. Crawl your site, crawl a competitor, and see what they have actually built that you have not: descriptions, title widths, one heading per page, structured data, alt text, and which tags are on which pages.
  • It compares what is implemented, not where anybody ranks. A rank is somebody else’s estimate and there is nothing you can do with it. “They put a description on every page and you do on five” is the same conversation with the work attached.
  • Everything is read from the page source of a public site, so it needs no account, no login and nothing from the other site’s owner.
  • Every figure is a share of the pages read, with both page counts printed above the table, so a six page site and a two hundred page site still compare. A gap under ten points is called much the same rather than turned into a finding.
  • Where either site runs a tag container, the room says so: a tag fired from inside a container is invisible in page source, and it will not let you tell a prospect they have no pixel on that basis.

2.43.1

  • Fixed: the calendar produced a correct order and a useless plan. The first real run on a 65 page site gave 38 dates that all read “write the description on”, because descriptions outrank the smaller fixes and sorting by severity stacks them. Faults still come strictly first, and after that no more than two tasks of one kind land in a row.
  • Fixed: it scheduled work on Christmas Day. 25 December and 1 January are skipped. Nothing else, because guessing at holidays across countries would be worse than leaving your calendar alone.

2.43.0

  • New: a Calendar room. Pick a start date and a pace, and it lays out a dated plan where every entry is a real finding from your own crawl, worst first: broken pages, then pages nothing links to, then missing descriptions, then the smaller fixes.
  • With Search Console connected it also schedules the searches this site already ranks eleven to twenty for, which is the cheapest work on any site: the page exists, people are already searching, and page two is one revision from page one.
  • Generic content ideas appear only once every real finding is scheduled, which on most sites is never. That is the difference between this and a calendar template.
  • Download the whole plan as a CSV that opens straight in Excel or Sheets.
  • The crawl now also reports thin pages, counted from the word count it already recorded.

2.42.0

  • Fixed: rooms could not be reached. The room bar had no way to handle more rooms than fit, so on a 1280 pixel screen Campaigns, Clients and Reports sat past the right edge with no way to scroll to them. The bar now scrolls sideways, a mouse wheel over it works, and the edge fades while there is more to reach.
  • The map colour key is one pill that opens, instead of six labels that were hidden on any screen under 1100 pixels, which is the width the console runs at inside your dashboard. The key was missing exactly where it was needed most.
  • Each colour now says what it means. “orphan” reads “orphan, nothing on the site links to it”.

2.41.0

  • New: Landing pages in the Visitors card and in the printed report. It shows the page each visit STARTED on, with its bounce rate beside it, because traffic with a high bounce is a page that is found and does not hold while no traffic at all is a page that is not found, and those need opposite work.
  • Site verification tokens are covered on screen now, with a Show the tokens box. They are not secrets, they are published on your own site by design; covering them keeps them out of screenshots and screen recordings.

2.40.0

  • New: a Clients room in the console. It says which site is yours and which are clients, shows what each one last scored and when, and audits any of them in one press. Your own site is whichever address is in your business profile, or whichever you mark by hand.
  • The roster builds itself: every site you crawl lands there. Add one by hand to keep it on the list before you have crawled it.
  • Your own site can show its visits, bounce rate and where people came from, read from the Analytics connection on this site. Client sites cannot, because nobody has an Analytics account for a site they do not run, and the room says so rather than showing an empty panel.
  • The printed report can carry a Visitors section, and it appears only when the crawl is of your own site AND the numbers were read for that same address. Crawling a client never prints your numbers on their report.

2.39.0

  • New: Visitors and where they came from, on the Credentials tab. With your Google account connected it reads your own Analytics property and shows visits, people, bounce rate, average visit length, pages seen, and anything bought, for the last 28 complete days.
  • It separates the two questions that get confused: traffic acquisition is where each visit came from, user acquisition is where each person first came from. Each table says which it is.
  • Figures end yesterday. Today is a part day, and including it would make every number quietly wrong by however many hours have passed.
  • If this site connected to Google before Analytics was part of the plugin, the card says so and tells you to press Connect Google again, instead of showing an error. Search Console keeps working either way.
  • The console can read Analytics, searches and speed in one call now, and each part says whether it can answer rather than reporting zero.

2.38.2

  • Fixed: 2.38.1 read Stape’s success message as an error. A good answer from Stape carries “All good” in the same place a failure puts its reason, so the container list showed “Stape answered with an error: All good”. Only a failure code counts as an error now.

2.38.1

  • Fixed: connecting Stape said an account with a container had none. Stape’s API wraps every answer in an envelope that its own documentation leaves off the container list, and the plugin read the envelope as if it were the list. It reads what is inside now, uses Stape’s default address when a container has no custom domain, and if Stape ever answers in a shape it cannot read, it says what arrived instead of calling the account empty.
  • Fixed: Cerebro sent its server side events to the bare root of your server container, where no client listens, so every forward and every test answered 400. They go to /data now, the address the Data Client by Stape listens on, in the same format as Stape’s own PHP library. Your server container needs the Data Client installed, and a 400 on the test now says so.
  • The purchase event sends its product count as item_count instead of items, which is GA4’s name for the list of products itself.

2.38.0

  • Every room and every dashboard tab is on the same cards now. Repairs, Redirector and Schema join the rooms converted in 2.37.0, and in your dashboard so do Settings, Schema, the Audit Inbox, Accessibility and the three tabs that moved into the console. Each card says what is true and what to press next, the settings wait in a drawer, and the explanations are one tap away.
  • In Repairs, each finding shows its fix up front, with why it ranks where it does, what links to it and the cause one tap away. Copying the AI brief is the first thing in the room.
  • A Security and your responsibility note, under every dashboard tab, in the console’s Settings and in this readme: these tools hold powerful keys, every release is checked with the official Plugin Check tool from WordPress, no software is flawless, and your own browser, devices and accounts are yours to keep safe.
  • Fixed: opening the Schema room in the docked console wiped the WordPress schema card for the rest of the session. The room is built once now, so it stays.
  • Fixed: on a phone, the More rooms list ran each room name into its description.
  • Fixed: on a laptop with a touch screen, including inside the dashboard, the Arcade collapsed to its heading and the game could not be seen.
  • Fixed: the Cerebro, Insights and Error Report tabs still pointed at a panel under Structure. They point at the Tracking room, where those blocks moved in 2.37.0.
  • The readme listed four rooms. It lists all of them now.

Earlier releases are in changelog.txt beside this file. They were moved there rather than deleted: the readme changelog is capped at 5,000 characters and this history is worth more than the cap.

short_description: Map your site like a planet. Crawl and grade structure, keep business listings consistent, fix broken pages, and ship valid schema.
description:
Your website is a planet. The Pods map it.

PSM SEO Site Console docks a complete, private first SEO toolkit inside your WordPress dashboard. Everything runs in your browser and on your own server. Nothing you type is uploaded to us, ever.

The rooms

  • Structure. Send the Pods to your site and they chart every path in a top down sitemap or a rotating 3D galaxy, surface orphan and broken pages, and hand back a letter grade. The same site always earns the same grade, so you can measure a fix.
  • Presence. One canonical business profile, checked field by field against the 11 directories that matter: Google Business Profile, LinkedIn, Bing Places, Apple Business Connect, Clutch, and more. Your data stays on your device.
  • Redirector. Broken pages found by the crawl become ready 301 rules, exportable as .htaccess directives or JSON.
  • Schema. Generate valid JSON-LD from your business profile, and inspect the structured data any page already ships.
  • Repairs. Every fault the crawl found, worst first, each with its cause and its fix, plus a brief to paste into an AI assistant.
  • Campaigns. Tagged links, so you can tell which channel actually brought someone.
  • Reports. What changed between two real crawls, and a report you can print or save as a PDF.
  • Tracking and Search engines. Inside your dashboard only: your own tag and its health, proving the site is yours to each search engine, instant indexing, and country versions.

The mothership features

  • Automatic structured data on your site: one clean schema graph covering your business entity, articles, products, FAQ, events, and video, each type toggleable.
  • A virtual XML sitemap served at /sitemap.xml with zero physical files written to disk.
  • Insights: your own first party, anonymous usage analytics with charts: headline stats, a six month trend, per surface totals, and a feature leaderboard, all on your server. No third party analytics, no identifiers, and Do Not Track is honored.
  • Cerebro: optional server side event forwarding to your own Google Tag Manager server container, plus a downloadable GTM recipe.
  • Webhook broadcasts of crawl findings to Zapier, Make, or n8n.
  • A diagnostics tab that decodes every error code in plain language.

Free and paid

This plugin is free and fully functional: crawl and grade your site structure, the complete Presence workflow, all schema tools, the virtual sitemap, Insights, Cerebro, webhooks, and the Search Console connection. Nothing here is gated behind a purchase. Planet Social Console Pro is a separate add on, installed alongside this plugin from our own site, that adds higher crawl caps and the large site skeleton crawl for very large sites.

Security and your responsibility

Planet Social Marketing is an independent developer. This plugin is not made, reviewed or endorsed by WordPress or the WordPress Foundation.

It connects your site to other services with keys and access you provide, such as a Google sign in, API keys and connect keys. Those are powerful: anyone who holds one can act as your site with that service. Keep them private, replace any key that leaks, and remove connections you no longer use.

We check every release against WordPress coding and security standards with the official Plugin Check tool from WordPress, and fix what it finds before we ship. No software is flawless, though, and this plugin is provided as is, without warranty, under the GPL.

We are not responsible for the security of your own browser, devices, hosting, accounts or passwords, or for faults in other plugins and services. Keep WordPress, your plugins and your browser up to date, use strong passwords and two factor sign in, and connect only services you trust.

Privacy

Crawls run in your browser. Your business profile lives in your browser’s local storage. The plugin stores its settings in a single option row and removes everything on uninstall. Optional anonymous feature counts go only to your own site’s endpoint. Full policy: https://planetsocialmarketing.com/privacy

External services

This plugin talks to the outside services listed below, each only for the purpose described. Your crawl results, page content, and business profile are never sent to us. Every service other than the web font is off until you choose to use it.

  1. Google Fonts (fonts.googleapis.com, fonts.gstatic.com).

The docked console interface loads its typefaces (Fraunces, Inter, and JetBrains Mono) from the Google Fonts CDN when you open the console screen in wp-admin. This is a request for font files only; your browser sends the standard request headers (including your IP address) to Google to fetch the fonts. No plugin data, page content, or profile information is included. If you prefer no external font request, the interface falls back to your system fonts.

This service is provided by Google LLC. Terms: https://policies.google.com/terms . Privacy: https://policies.google.com/privacy

  1. Google APIs, optional and off until you enable them.

If you connect Google on the Credentials tab, your browser goes to accounts.google.com so you can approve access, and the plugin exchanges, refreshes and, when you disconnect, revokes the resulting tokens at oauth2.googleapis.com. With that connection it reads your own verified Search Console property from www.googleapis.com, and asks searchconsole.googleapis.com how Google sees a page when you inspect one. With the same connection it reads your own Google Analytics property: analyticsadmin.googleapis.com says which properties your account has and which web address each one measures, so the plugin can find the one that belongs to this site, and analyticsdata.googleapis.com returns visit counts, bounce rate, average visit length, where visits and visitors came from, and anything bought, for whole days only. Every one of these calls only reads: the plugin never creates, changes or deletes anything in Analytics or Search Console, and no page content or visitor record leaves your site. Sites connected before Analytics was added granted Search Console only and keep working; reading Analytics needs you to press Connect Google again and approve it. If you set up Cerebro server side tagging, the events you select are forwarded to the Google Tag Manager server container that you own and control, at the address you enter. If you enter your Google Tag Manager container ID and turn on Load GTM on the site, the plugin loads that container from www.googletagmanager.com on your front end, the same snippet you would otherwise paste by hand. All of these stay dormant until you configure them, and you can turn them off at any time. Data flows only between your own site and your own Google account.

This service is provided by Google LLC. Terms: https://policies.google.com/terms . Privacy: https://policies.google.com/privacy

  1. Google Tag Manager API, optional and off until you switch on Tag Manager writing.

Only if you switch on Tag Manager writing under Cerebro and connect Google does the plugin ask Google for permission to edit your Tag Manager containers (the tagmanager.edit.containers scope). With it, the plugin asks tagmanager.googleapis.com which containers your account can edit, so you can pick one by name. Then, only when you press Build the tags, it creates one new workspace in the container you chose and adds a GA4 configuration tag, plus a trigger and an event tag for each event in the set you picked. What is sent is the container address, your GA4 measurement ID and those tag and trigger definitions. It never publishes: the plugin does not ask for permission to publish a container, so nothing it creates reaches your visitors until you review the workspace in Tag Manager and publish it yourself. It never changes or deletes a tag or trigger that was already there. Show me what it would build lists the same objects and sends nothing. While the switch is off, the permission is not requested at all.

This service is provided by Google LLC. Terms: https://policies.google.com/terms . Privacy: https://policies.google.com/privacy

  1. Stape, optional and off until you connect it.

If you paste a Stape API key on the Credentials tab, the plugin asks Stape which server containers your account has and what addresses they answer on, so you can pick one by name instead of copying a long address by hand. Only the key is sent, as a header, to api.app.stape.io or api.app.eu.stape.io depending on the region you choose. Every call is read only: the plugin never creates, changes or deletes anything in your Stape account. No page content, crawl result or visitor data is involved. The key is stored encrypted with your site keys, and Disconnect removes it.

This service is provided by Stape. Terms: https://stape.io/terms-conditions . Privacy: https://stape.io/privacy-notice

  1. Google PageSpeed Insights, optional and off until you connect it.

If you paste a PageSpeed Insights API key on the Credentials tab, then each time you press the check button the plugin sends one page address and the key to www.googleapis.com and receives back how fast that page is. Google answers with two different things and the plugin keeps them apart: what real Chrome visitors experienced over the last 28 days, which only exists where enough people visited, and a simulation run on Google’s own hardware. Nothing is sent unless you press the button, and only the address of a page on your own site is ever sent.

This service is provided by Google LLC. Terms: https://policies.google.com/terms . Privacy: https://policies.google.com/privacy

  1. IndexNow, optional and off until you switch it on.

IndexNow tells search engines that a page on your site changed, so they read it again sooner instead of waiting for their next crawl. While it is switched on, the plugin sends a request to api.indexnow.org when a public post is published, unpublished or moved to the trash, when the Planet Social Redirector plugin creates a permanent redirect (the old address and the new one), and when you press one of the IndexNow buttons in the console (your home page, or your twenty most recently published posts). Each request carries your site’s host name, the addresses of those pages, your site’s IndexNow key and the address of its key file. The key is not a secret: the plugin publishes it at your site’s root so the engines can confirm the request came from your site. The same address is not sent again within an hour. IndexNow shares each submission with the search engines taking part, such as Microsoft Bing, Yandex, Seznam and Naver. No page content and no visitor data is sent.

IndexNow is run by its sponsors, Microsoft, Yandex and Seznam.cz. Terms: https://www.indexnow.org/terms . Privacy: the Privacy section of the same page, https://www.indexnow.org/terms

  1. Webhook automation, only the address you enter.

If you paste a webhook URL on the Credentials tab, for example a Zapier catch hook at hooks.zapier.com or a Make or n8n webhook, the plugin POSTs a small JSON summary of crawl findings to that address when a broadcast fires. Nothing is sent until you enter a URL, and it goes only to the endpoint you chose, under that service’s own terms. Zapier terms: https://zapier.com/legal/terms-of-service . Zapier privacy: https://zapier.com/privacy

  1. Crawl relay, only the address you enter.

Crawling the site this plugin is installed on happens directly in your browser. Browsers block reading other sites that way, so to crawl a different site, such as a client’s, you can run a small relay of your own and enter its address under Advanced in the console. The console then sends the address of each page it wants to read to your relay, which fetches that page from the site you chose and hands it back. Nothing goes to a relay until you enter one. The setup guide uses a free Cloudflare Worker, at an address like your-worker.workers.dev, which is also the hint shown in the empty field. Cloudflare terms: https://www.cloudflare.com/website-terms/ . Cloudflare privacy: https://www.cloudflare.com/privacypolicy/

  1. Business directory links, in the Presence room.

The Presence room lists eleven business directories as ordinary links. The plugin never connects to them, fetches from them or sends them anything. A directory opens in a new tab only when you click it, and from then on you are on that site under its own terms.

  • Google Business Profile, business.google.com. Terms: https://policies.google.com/terms . Privacy: https://policies.google.com/privacy
  • LinkedIn Company Page, www.linkedin.com. Terms: https://www.linkedin.com/legal/user-agreement . Privacy: https://www.linkedin.com/legal/privacy-policy
  • Bing Places, www.bingplaces.com. Terms: https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/servicesagreement . Privacy: https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/privacy/privacystatement
  • Apple Business Connect, businessconnect.apple.com. Terms: https://www.apple.com/legal/internet-services/terms/site.html . Privacy: https://www.apple.com/legal/privacy/en-ww/
  • Clutch, clutch.co. Terms: https://clutch.co/terms . Privacy: https://clutch.co/privacy
  • Yelp for Business, biz.yelp.com. Terms: https://www.yelp.com/static?p=tos . Privacy: https://www.yelp.com/static?p=privacy
  • Facebook Business Page, www.facebook.com. Terms: https://www.facebook.com/terms/ . Privacy: https://www.facebook.com/privacy/policy/
  • Foursquare, business.foursquare.com. Terms: https://foursquare.com/legal/terms . Privacy: https://foursquare.com/legal/privacy
  • YellowPages, accounts.yellowpages.com. Terms: https://www.yellowpages.com/about/legal/terms-conditions . Privacy: https://www.yellowpages.com/privacy
  • Better Business Bureau, www.bbb.org. Terms: https://www.bbb.org/terms-of-use . Privacy: https://www.bbb.org/privacy-policy
  • Nextdoor Business, business.nextdoor.com. Terms and privacy: Nextdoor’s Member Agreement and Privacy Policy, in the Legal section of the Nextdoor Help Center, which the foot of nextdoor.com links to.
  1. Other links.

These are ordinary links too. Nothing is sent until you click one.

  • The Pods app on Google Play, play.google.com, and on the Amazon Appstore, www.amazon.com. Google Play terms: https://play.google.com/about/play-terms/index.html . Google privacy: https://policies.google.com/privacy . Amazon conditions of use: https://www.amazon.com/gp/help/customer/display.html?nodeId=GLSBYFE9MGKKQXXM . Amazon privacy: https://www.amazon.com/gp/help/customer/display.html?nodeId=GX7NJQ4ZB8MHFRNJ
  • Google’s Rich Results Test at search.google.com, and your own Google Analytics and Tag Manager at analytics.google.com and tagmanager.google.com, under the Google terms and privacy policy in item 2.
  • The Schema Markup Validator at validator.schema.org, part of schema.org. Terms: https://schema.org/docs/terms.html . The validator publishes no separate privacy policy.
  • Our own site, planetsocialmarketing.com, for the field manual, the relay guide, plans and our policies. Terms: https://planetsocialmarketing.com/terms-of-service/ . Privacy: https://planetsocialmarketing.com/privacy/

Addresses on schema.org, www.w3.org and www.sitemaps.org that appear in the code are the names of vocabularies and formats written into your pages and your sitemap; the plugin never contacts them. Addresses on example.com and other reserved example names appear only as hints inside empty fields.
